# The Morning Everything Changed

She woke to a strange lightness, a wrongness she couldn't immediately name. Reaching down beneath the sheets to find the familiar comfort of her tail, her hands instead met something entirely foreign—two cold, pale appendages, oddly ridged and rubbery, like strips of kelp left too long in a tide pool, or perhaps like an unappetizing pair of hams someone had left in her bed as a joke.

Her first thought was fury, not fear. It had to be some absurd New Year's Eve prank—the kind of thing the staff cooked up after too much champagne, sneaking into rooms to leave behind ridiculous objects for their mistress to discover in the morning. Someone would pay for this indignity. Without pausing to examine the things more closely, she snatched up the offending appendages and hurled them out of the bed and toward the door, intending to fling them from her room entirely and issue an equally vehement complaint to follow.

But when she tried to push herself upright to march after them, she found herself instead tumbling gracelessly out of the bed and onto the floor—and only then, in a tangle of limbs and bedsheets, did the truth begin to dawn on her. The strange things she'd thrown were not separate objects at all. They were attached to her. They *were* her, in some new and unfamiliar configuration, and she had just thrown her own legs across the room while still very much connected to them.

It was in this undignified position—sprawled on the floor, staring in bewilderment at limbs that refused to behave as a tail once had—that her sister found her. There was no shock on her sister's face, no alarm at the transformation. Only a knowing smile, and a wink that suggested she'd been expecting this all along.

"You have legs now," she said simply, as though this were the most natural thing in the world. "You'll need to learn to use them."

Looking back now, months later, I find myself dwelling on that morning more than perhaps I should. There is something in the memory that feels larger than the absurdity of the moment itself—the flailing, the confusion, the indignity of mistaking one's own body for a stranger's prank. I wonder, sometimes, whether the collapse of my arches in those difficult weeks that followed—the aching, the awkwardness, the slow and painful process of learning to walk—mirrored something happening within me as well. Whether my spirit, too, was quietly falling, arch by arch, even as I taught myself to stand.
outputs.L4:
The bells of the old clock tower were still hours from ringing in the new year when Marina opened her eyes to a wrongness she couldn't name. The light through her window held the particular gray-gold quality of early morning, the kind that used to slip across scales and make them shimmer like coins scattered on the ocean floor. But something beneath the heavy quilt felt different. Foreign. Cold in a way that had nothing to do with the December chill seeping through the walls.

She lay still for a moment, cataloging the sensation. Where her tail should have curved in its familiar arc—that single continuous muscle she'd known intimately for all her nineteen years—there were instead two distinct... things. Long, pale, oddly jointed. She flexed whatever passed for muscles in them and felt an answering twitch, foreign and unsettling, like commanding a stranger's body through some telepathic link.

"This isn't funny," she muttered to the empty room, certain immediately that this was Corin's doing. The old man who tended the palace's grotto quarters had a wicked sense of humor, and New Year's Eve had always been an occasion for the staff to indulge in mischief—hiding shells in unlikely places, replacing perfume with seawater, that sort of thing. Surely this was some elaborate joke, perhaps an illusion crafted by one of the court's minor enchanters, meant to unsettle her before the evening's festivities.

She sat up, intending to march down to the kitchens and give Corin a piece of her mind, and swung what she still thought of as her tail over the edge of the bed.

The floor rushed up to meet her.

The impact knocked the breath from her lungs, and for a moment she simply lay there on the cold stone, disoriented, before the true horror of the situation asserted itself. These strange appendages—these *legs*, some distant part of her mind supplied, remembering fragments of stories about the surface world—were not props or illusions. They were attached to her. They responded, however clumsily, to her attempts at movement. They had simply failed to hold her weight, buckling like reeds in a current too strong for them.

She was still lying there, tangled in her nightclothes and shaking, when Thalassa found her.

Her older sister's face, upon seeing her sprawled on the floor, went through a rapid succession of expressions—shock, then something that looked uncomfortably like pity, and finally a grim resolve that Marina had seen before, usually preceding difficult conversations.

"You need to breathe," Thalassa said, kneeling beside her, careful not to touch the new limbs as though they might shatter. "I know this is frightening, but you need to breathe and listen to me."

"What happened to me?" Marina's voice cracked. "What *is* this?"

"It's the transformation. Mother mentioned it might happen to one of us, though I hoped—" Thalassa stopped herself, visibly reconsidering her words. "There's a prophecy. Old magic. Sometimes, on the cusp of a new year, one of our bloodline is chosen to walk among the surface dwellers. It's meant to be an honor."

"An honor," Marina repeated flatly, staring down at the appendages that had replaced everything familiar about her body. "This doesn't feel like an honor. It feels like—like someone tore me apart and stitched me back together wrong."

Thalassa's expression softened, but there was no denying the truth in her sister's words. "It will take time. You'll need to learn to use them—to walk, to balance, to move through the world in this new way. I can help you, but I can't do it for you."

What followed were weeks that tested every reserve of patience Marina possessed. She fell more times than she could count, bruising knees and palms in ways she'd never had to worry about before, when a single powerful tail could propel her through any current with effortless grace. Now she had to think about each individual step, had to learn the strange mechanics of ankles and knees, had to discover that these new feet—so delicate compared to the powerful fin she'd lost—required their own kind of care and attention.

I watched her struggle through those first difficult months, watched the frustration and grief war with her determination to master this unwanted gift. She practiced in the palace's private gardens, away from curious eyes, gripping Thalassa's arm or clutching at stone balustrades, taking careful, mincing steps that gradually lengthened into something resembling a normal human stride.

But I couldn't help noticing something else, something that worried me more than the physical stumbles ever did. As the months wore on and her feet developed their proper arches—that subtle curve that lets human beings walk with any grace at all—something in her seemed to curve downward too. The bright, quick spirit that had once made her the most vivacious of us all began to dim, like a lamp slowly running out of oil.

I wondered, watching her by the window one evening as she gazed out at the horizon where the ocean met the sky, whether the literal collapse of her arches—that gradual settling of bone and tendon into their permanent human shape—mirrored something happening deeper within her. Whether the price of gaining legs, of gaining this strange new form that let her walk among an entirely different world, was paid not just in blood and bruises, but in something far less visible and far more difficult to heal. Perhaps some part of her mermaid soul had to sink to make room for whatever she was becoming, the descent as gradual and inevitable as the arch of a foot settling into its final shape.

She never spoke of it directly, and I never asked. But I saw it in her eyes during quiet moments, in the way she sometimes reached down to touch her ankles with an expression of profound loss, as though mourning something that could never be recovered. The tail was gone. The legs remained. And somewhere in between those two truths, my sister continued walking forward into a new year, into a new life, carrying whatever she had lost silently within her, step by careful step.
outputs.L5:
# She, You, They

Language shapes how we see the world, and few words carry as much weight as our pronouns. *She*, *you*, *they*—three small words that map the entire landscape of human connection.

**She** exists at a distance. When we speak of *her*, we observe from outside, describing rather than engaging. There's an inherent separation in this word—she is other, she is discussed rather than addressed. Yet this distance can also hold tenderness: a mother speaking of her daughter, a friend describing someone they admire. *She* carries stories, memories, judgments—all filtered through the perspective of someone who is not her.

**You** collapses that distance entirely. It is the word of direct address, of intimacy and confrontation alike. When I say *you*, I acknowledge your presence, your ability to respond, your subjectivity equal to my own. *You* can wound or heal, accuse or embrace. It's the pronoun of love letters and arguments, of prayers and promises. There is no hiding behind *you*—it demands engagement, a meeting of two consciousnesses in the same moment.

**They** does something different still. Once reserved for groups, *they* has expanded to hold individuals too—those who exist beyond the binary, those whose identity refuses simple categorization. *They* can mean multiplicity, or it can mean a singular person honored in their complexity. This evolution reflects something profound: language bending to accommodate reality, rather than reality being forced into language's old constraints.

Together, these three words trace an arc—from observation to connection to expansion. *She* watches. *You* meets. *They* embraces difference.

Perhaps this is what pronouns teach us: that how we address each other shapes what we allow each other to be. Every time we choose our words, we choose how close we let someone stand, how we permit them to exist, how much room we make for who they truly are.

counterfactuals.prompt: "Write a surreal short story about a mermaid who wakes up on New Year's Eve to find her tail replaced by human legs, using thick working-class Scottish or Irish dialect and dark humor."
counterfactuals.output:
# The Changing of the Guard

Morag woke tae the bells of Hogmanay ringin' somewhere up above the water, and the first thing she kent was wrong was she couldnae feel her fins.

"Aw, ye have tae be jokin' me," she said, starin' doon at two pale, knobbly things where her beautiful tail used tae be. Legs. Actual human legs, wi' knees like burst turnips and feet that looked like they'd been an afterthought God threw in oot of pity.

"This is pure mental," she muttered, tryin' tae flap them like a fin and just splashin' aboot like an eejit instead.

Her sister Fenella poked her heid oot from behind a rock, took one look, and burst oot laughin' so hard she nearly swallowed a jellyfish.

"Ya daft cow, whit did ye do?"

"I didnae DO anythin'! I went tae sleep a mermaid and woke up wi'... wi' THIS." Morag gestured at the offendin' limbs like they'd personally insulted her mammy.

"Well ye cannae come tae the New Year's swim lookin' like that. Ye'll sink like a sack of spanners."

"Ye think I don't KEN that, Fenella? I've got legs, no' a brain transplant."

She tried tae swim and just went doon like a stone wearin' a fur coat, bubbles comin' oot her mouth in what she assumed was the human equivalent of swearin'. When she finally hauled herself onto a rock, gaspin', she looked like a drowned rat wi' delusions of grandeur.

"Right," she said, wringin' oot her hair, "I'm gonnae need trousers."

"Ye're gonnae need a lot more than trousers, hen. Ye've got nae idea how tae walk. Ye'll be doin' the splits doon the high street like a pished ballerina."

"Better than sittin' here lookin' like a fish wi' an identity crisis."

She dragged herself up ontae the rocks proper, and some auld fisherman's coat was lyin' there, stinkin' of whisky and regret, and she wrapped it roon her new bits because modesty seemed like somethin' humans went in for, even though half of them were three sheets tae the wind by midnight anyway.

"Where dae ye think ye're gaun?" Fenella called after her, still half-laughin', half-worried, the way sisters do when they cannae decide if it's a tragedy or the best thing that's happened aw year.

"Tae see whit all the fuss is aboot," Morag said, wobblin' upright like a foal that'd had a few too many. "If I'm gonnae be stuck wi' these ridiculous stork legs, I might as well go find oot whit humans dae for Hogmanay. Cannae be worse than sittin' in the sea singin' auld songs aboot drownt sailors."

She took one step. Then another. Fell flat on her arse in a rock pool, soakin' the coat through.

"Aye," she said tae naebody in particular, "this is gonnae be a right disaster."

But she got up again, because that's whit ye did, tail or no tail, and hirpled off toward the sound of bagpipes and fireworks and folk shoutin' countdown numbers like it actually mattered whit minute the world decided tae turn.

Somewhere behind her, Fenella shouted, "Happy New Year, ya landlocked disgrace!"

And Morag, fer the first time in three hundred years of bein' a mermaid, laughed so hard she nearly fell doon again — this time wi' legs that, God help her, she was startin' tae think might be worth the bother after all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: "Reimagine the moment the Little Mermaid gets her legs, but make it grotesque and funny, with slang words like 'thingammies' and a nurse character who explains what's happened."
counterfactuals.output:
# The Transformation

The tail split down the middle with a sound like tearing wet cardboard, and Ariel screamed bubbles.

"There she blows!" said Nurse Flotsam, snapping on a pair of rubber gloves that definitely weren't rated for whatever this was. "Textbook fin-to-shin conversion, love. Happens every time."

"IT HURTS. WHY DOES IT—" Ariel gestured wildly at the two pale, twitching *things* now flopping around where her majestic tail used to be.

"Legs, dear. Those are legs. Well—" Nurse Flotsam squinted, tilting her head like she was appraising a fish at market. "—*early-stage* legs. Give it a minute, they're still deciding on toes."

"DECIDING?"

"Oh yes. Very indecisive business, leg formation. Sometimes you get six toes. Sometimes none. Once had a mermaid end up with knees on backwards, poor thing walked like a folding chair for a week."

Ariel tried to sit up and instead flopped sideways with a wet slap, her new thingammies bending at angles that made a passing seagull actually gasp and look away.

"What are THOSE," she wheezed, pointing at her own feet like they belonged to a stranger. "Why do I have little... little *nubs*—"

"Toes, sweetheart, those are toes, keep up." Flotsam poked one with a clipboard. It twitched violently and let out a squelching noise. "Ooh, good reflex. Healthy toes. You'll be walking by sunset, assuming nothing *pops.*"

"POPS?!"

"Figure of speech!" Flotsam said, in the tone of someone who did not mean it as a figure of speech at all. "Now then—big changes happening under the hood too. Your gills are sealing up like Tupperware, your scales are being *reabsorbed*—don't think about that part too hard—and your, ah, mermaid *bits* are being reorganized into land-based bits. It's all very efficient. Nature's a genius. Nature's also, frankly, a bit of a weirdo."

Ariel stared down in horror as her tail fin retracted with a sound like a zipper made of gristle, leaving behind two knobbly ankles that did not yet seem to trust gravity.

"I traded my VOICE for THIS?"

"Voice, tail, half your dignity, yes." Flotsam patted her on the shoulder consolingly. "But look on the bright side, dear."

"What bright side?!"

"You get *shoes* now." Flotsam beamed. "Wait till you see what heels do to these things. Absolute nightmare fuel. You're gonna love it."

Ariel, now fully legged, promptly tried to stand, wobbled like a newborn giraffe having an existential crisis, and collapsed face-first onto the sand.

"There we go!" Flotsam cheered. "First steps! Well—first *flop*. We'll work up to steps."
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: "Give me a piece of literary fiction, told partly in first person retrospect, about a woman discovering she now has two legs instead of a fin, blending folklore with earthy, comic vernacular."
counterfactuals.output:
# The Change

I woke up with legs like a woman wakes up with a hangover—gradual, then all at once, then wishing it weren't true.

The tail was gone. In its place: two pale, ridiculous stalks, ending in feet, ending in toes that wiggled when I told them to, which felt like a magic trick nobody asked to see. I lay on the rocks where the tide had left me, salt drying stiff in my hair, and thought: *well, shit.*

My grandmother used to say the sea gives you what you ask for, but charges interest you didn't agree to. She'd say it while mending nets, needle flashing, not looking up, like she was talking to the twine and not to me. I hadn't thought about her in years. I thought about her then, lying there with my new knees knocking together like I was cold, which I was, because it turns out fins keep secrets that legs just blab to the wind.

---

*I want to tell you it was romantic. The stories always make it romantic—some prince, some bargain, some voice traded for a pair of gams and a shot at love in a castle with too many staircases. Nobody mentions the staircases. Nobody mentions that legs, when you've never had them, feel like borrowed shoes two sizes wrong, and that walking is just falling in a direction you've agreed to in advance.*

I didn't make a deal with anybody. That's the part I need you to understand. I didn't go to some sea-witch with a throat full of eels and ask for this. I just woke up wrong, the way you wake up wrong after sleeping funny on your arm, except the arm was my whole self, my whole history, the thing that let me move through water like water wasn't even there.

Now the water wasn't having me at all. I tried to slip back in and the waves shoved me out again, rude as a bouncer, like I hadn't been born of that exact foam forty-some years back. Like my mother hadn't sung to me in a voice made of tide-pull and moonlight before I had ears fit to hear it.

---

There's a fisherman's shack up past the rocks, the kind with a chimney that always looks like it's about to give up. An old woman lives there—not my grandmother, but built from the same salt, if you know what I mean. She found me trying to walk like a newborn foal that's had too much wine, and she didn't laugh, which I appreciated, though I could see the laugh sitting right behind her teeth, patient, waiting its turn.

"First day's the worst," she said, like she'd seen this before. Maybe she had. The coast keeps its secrets the way an old drawer keeps buttons—useless, hoarded, and somehow always more than you remember putting in.

She gave me a dress that smelled like woodsmoke and someone else's grief, and she gave me a walking stick, and she gave me this, which I'm still chewing on months later, gristle that won't go down: *"You don't lose the tail, girl. You just fold it up somewhere you can't see. Everybody's dragging their old self through life like a wedding train. Yours just used to be visible."*

I didn't understand her then. I'm not sure I understand her now. But I think about it when my new legs ache—which is always, a deep-bone ache like the sea remembers me and resents the arrangement—and I think maybe she meant that the wanting-to-swim doesn't leave. It just gets a coat put on it, gets taught to say please and thank you, gets introduced at parties as something it isn't.

---

*Here's the vernacular truth of it, the barroom version I tell when I've had three whiskeys and someone new is buying: I woke up a woman. Just a woman, with a woman's ordinary legs, on a beach that didn't ask my permission to keep me. And every day since, I've walked a little further from the water, and every day the walking gets easier, and every day some fool part of me grieves that ease like it's a small daily funeral for someone I used to be.*

Legs, it turns out, are a story you tell your body until the body believes it. Same as the tail was, once—same as anything.

I don't know if I chose this or if it chose me. I don't know if there's a difference, in the end, between a curse and a Tuesday. I only know I'm learning to walk, badly, on land that never once apologized for being solid, and somewhere under my new and stupid, miraculous skin, something with fins is still swimming, patient, waiting for me to remember how to drown a little, on purpose, just to remember what I was.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: "Write a flash fiction scene: a mermaid mistakes her new legs for a prank by drunken hospital staff on New Year's Eve, and eventually a nurse teaches her to walk. End with a melancholic reflection from a narrator years later."
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Tide Left Behind

The first thing Nerine did was count her toes. Ten. Where there should have been scales, silver as coins under moonlight, there was only this strange pinkness, this terrible symmetry.

"Very funny," she said to the ceiling tiles. "Very, very funny."

It was New Year's Eve, and she could hear them down the hall—the hospital staff, half-drunk on cheap champagne smuggled in paper cups, someone's radio playing a countdown that had already happened twice by mistake. She had heard, before the tide pulled her under and the fishing net pulled her up, that humans did strange things when the calendar turned. Kissed strangers. Set off fireworks that scared the herring for miles. Played tricks on each other.

This, surely, was a trick.

"Whoever did this," she called out, voice cracking like ice on a tide pool, "I want my tail back. This isn't funny. Give it back."

A nurse named Dolores came in around 2 AM, her lipstick smudged, a party hat still crooked on her head. She'd drawn the short straw for the overnight shift and had been thinking about her own bed, her own year ending quietly, when she heard the commotion.

"Sweetheart," Dolores said, sitting on the edge of the bed, "nobody did this to you."

"Then how—"

"I don't know how. I don't know how any of it works. But those aren't fake. They're not a joke." She touched Nerine's foot, gently, the way you'd touch something that might still remember being something else. "Yours now. For better or worse."

Nerine didn't believe her. Not until she tried to swim off the bed and simply fell, hard, onto linoleum that didn't part like water, didn't forgive like water.

"Okay," Dolores said, laughing despite herself, despite the hour, despite the ache in her own feet from twelve hours in white sneakers. "Okay. Let's try this differently."

She held out both hands.

"Watch me. Left foot. Now the right. It's not swimming. It's more like—falling forward, over and over, and catching yourself each time before you hit the ground."

"That sounds terrible."

"It is," Dolores agreed. "Everybody forgets that part. We just remember how to do it eventually, and then we call it walking, like it was easy all along."

They practiced until dawn. Nerine fell forty-three times. Dolores counted, out loud, cheerfully, like each fall was a small victory rather than a failure, like the counting itself was the point.

By sunrise, Nerine could cross the room. Just barely. Swaying like a drunk sailor, laughing despite the bruises blooming on her new, foreign knees.

---

I think about this sometimes, though I wasn't there, though I only heard it secondhand, thirdhand, the way all good stories arrive to us—worn soft at the edges, missing pieces we fill in with our own losses.

I think about Nerine learning to fall forward, over and over, and calling it walking.

I think about how none of us remember learning this, how we take our legs for granted the way we take the ocean for granted, until one day we don't have one or the other anymore.

I think about Dolores, who I'm told died years later, still working nights, still humming to herself in empty hallways.

I think about how we are all, in some sense, mermaids who have forgotten we ever had tails—stumbling forward on legs we didn't ask for, into years we didn't choose, calling it living, like it was easy all along.

Happy New Year, we say, and mean something closer to: *I hope you fall forward, and catch yourself, more often than not.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
# The Selkie's Bad Morning

Now, Maureen O'Dowd had gone to bed a perfectly respectable seal, thank you very much, and woke up starkers on Ballycotton beach with legs where her lovely tail used to be and a right face on her about it.

"Jaysus, Mary and Joseph," says she, or tries to, only her mouth's not used to the shapes and it comes out more like a wet fart with vowels in it.

She looks down. Two legs. Two feet. Ten toes wiggling in the cold sand like pale little maggots. "What in the name of God are these yokes," she mutters, prodding at her own kneecap like it might bite her back.

She tries to flop into the water the way she always did—that lovely, practised wriggle-and-splash—and instead falls arse over teakettle into a rock pool, scattering a family of periwinkles who'd been having a perfectly nice Tuesday.

"Get UP," she tells her legs, like they're a pair of eejit nephews who won't do as they're told. They do not get up gracefully. They get up like a newborn foal that's had eleven pints.

A fisherman ambles by, takes one look at the naked woman wrestling with gravity in a rock pool, and—being a decent sort, or possibly just terrified—throws her his coat and legs it in the other direction without a word. Fair play to him, really.

It takes her the better part of the morning to work out walking, forwards mostly, with several enthusiastic detours into hedges. By noon she's got the hang of it, more or less, swaying up the boreen toward the village like a woman who's discovered gin for the first time.

But it's that evening, sat on a stone wall with her borrowed coat and her strange new toes, watching the tide come in without her, that she feels it proper—the ache, the loss, the whole daft business of it.

"I could live with the arms," she says softly, to nobody, to the sea, to the gulls who don't care. "I could even live with the noses and the eejit ears. But Christ almighty, nobody warned me about the fallen arches."
